questions.question: What is `ForceRetryError` and what information does it carry?
questions.answer:
`ForceRetryError` is the error Ky uses when you force a retry. If an `afterResponse` hook returns `ky.retry(...)`, Ky turns that into a `ForceRetryError` and runs the normal retry flow. Hooks can see it in `beforeRetry` and `beforeError`, and you can detect it with the `isForceRetryError()` type guard (`source/errors/ForceRetryError.ts:6-11`, `source/utils/type-guards.ts:101-155`). It extends `KyError`, the base class for Ky's own errors (`source/errors/KyError.ts:1-14`).

## What it carries

The constructor takes the same `ForceRetryOptions` you pass to `ky.retry()` and stores them on the error (`source/errors/ForceRetryError.ts:11-15, 48-50`):

| Property | Type | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | `'ForceRetryError'` | fixed |
| `code` | `string \| undefined` | `options.code`, a label you choose, e.g. `'RATE_LIMIT'` |
| `customDelay` | `number \| undefined` | `options.delay`, milliseconds to wait before retrying |
| `customRequest` | `Request \| undefined` | `options.request`, a different request to use for the retry |
| `message` | `string` | `'Forced retry'`, or `'Forced retry: <code>'` when a code is given |
| `cause` | `Error` (optional) | `options.cause`, which keeps the original error in the chain |

```ts
super(
	options?.code === undefined ? 'Forced retry' : `Forced retry: ${options.code}`,
	cause ? {cause} : undefined,
);
```
(`source/errors/ForceRetryError.ts:42-46`)

Some details:
- **Message:** an empty code still shows up, so `{code: ''}` gives `'Forced retry: '` (`test/retry.ts:5151-5158`).
- **Cause:** if `cause` isn't an `Error`, it gets wrapped with `NonError.wrap` (`source/errors/ForceRetryError.ts:38-40`). With no cause, the error has no own `cause` property at all (`test/errors.ts:103-106`).

## Validation

The constructor checks its options and throws a `TypeError` in these cases (`source/errors/ForceRetryError.ts:19-36`):
- `options` is `null`
- `delay` is not a non-negative number. `Infinity` is allowed, but negative values and `NaN` are rejected so they can't quietly cut the backoff to almost nothing.
- `code` is not a string
- `request` is not a `Request`. A `Request` from another realm is accepted.

## Example

The `ForceRetryOptions` docs describe the use cases: retry after a delay the API tells you, switch to a backup endpoint, or keep the error that triggered the retry (`source/core/constants.ts:101-157, 201-221`):

```ts
return ky.retry({
	code: 'VALIDATION_FAILED',
	cause: error, // becomes ForceRetryError.cause
});
```

The readme says forced retries still count against `retry.limit` but skip the `shouldRetry` check (`readme.md:1151-1153`).

questions.question: What is the difference between the `timeout` and `totalTimeout` options?
questions.answer:
`timeout` is a time limit for each attempt. `totalTimeout` is one time limit for the whole call, including every retry and the waits between retries. They can be used together, and whichever runs out first wins.

| | `timeout` | `totalTimeout` |
|---|---|---|
| What it covers | One attempt, "applied independently to each retry" | "the entire operation, including retries and delays" |
| Default | `10000` (10 s) | `false` (no overall limit) |
| Allowed values | A non-negative number or `false` | A non-negative number or `false` |

Both are documented in `source/types/options.ts:211-246`.

**How they work together.** Before each wait, Ky uses the smaller of `timeout` and whatever is left of the `totalTimeout` budget (`source/core/Ky.ts:868-877`):

```ts
const effectiveTimeout = Math.min(
  this.#options.timeout === false ? Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY : this.#options.timeout,
  remainingTotal);
```

- Each attempt is cut short if it uses up its own `timeout`, or if the overall budget runs out first.
- If no overall time is left when Ky checks, it throws a `TimeoutError` right away (`source/core/Ky.ts:870-873`).
- Ky also checks the overall budget after `fetch` returns or fails. If the budget is used up, it aborts the request, cancels the response body and throws a `TimeoutError` (`source/core/Ky.ts:1254-1265`).

**Other differences:**
- **Reading the body:** shortcut methods such as `.json()` also give the body read its own separate `timeout`. The remaining `totalTimeout` budget still limits that read (`source/types/options.ts:212`, `source/core/Ky.ts:881-896`).
- **Turning them off:** `timeout: false` removes the per-attempt limit. `totalTimeout` has no limit by default.
- **Error bodies:** when Ky reads the body of an error response and `timeout` is `false`, it still limits that read to 10 s, or less if `totalTimeout` has less time left (`source/core/Ky.ts:855-865`).
- **`beforeError` hooks:** `totalTimeout` does not limit these hooks (`source/types/options.ts:225`).
- **Invalid values:** both options are checked the same way. A value that isn't a number or `false` (including `NaN` or a negative number) throws a `TypeError`. A value above 2147483647, including `Infinity`, throws a `RangeError` (`source/core/Ky.ts:201-215`).

The documentation includes this example (`source/types/options.ts:235-243`):

```ts
// Each attempt gets 5s, but the whole operation must complete within 30s
await ky('https://example.com', {
  timeout: 5000,
  totalTimeout: 30_000,
  retry: {limit: 3, retryOnTimeout: true}
}).json();
```

questions.question: What does `replaceOption` do when extending an instance?
questions.answer:
`replaceOption(value)` tells `.extend()` to **replace** the parent instance's value for that option instead of merging into it. By default, `.extend()` deep-merges options: hooks are appended, headers are merged, search params pile up and signals are combined. Wrapping a value in `replaceOption()` turns that merge off for that one value (`source/utils/merge.ts:31-51`).

```ts
const base = ky.create({hooks: {beforeRequest: [addAuth, addTracking]}});
const extended = base.extend({
	hooks: replaceOption({beforeRequest: [onlyThis]}),
});
// hooks.beforeRequest is now [onlyThis], not [addAuth, addTracking, onlyThis]
```

**How it works.** `replaceOption` does not change your value. It wraps it in a small object tagged with a global symbol, `Symbol.for('ky.replaceOption')`. Because the symbol is global, a wrapper made by a second, duplicated copy of Ky is still recognised (`source/utils/merge.ts:53-61`). During merging, `getReplaceState()` checks for that tag. It returns the unwrapped value plus an `isReplace` flag (`source/utils/merge.ts:20-29`). The merge in `deepMergeInternal` then handles `isReplace` differently for each option:

- **Generic deep-merged options:** a wrapped value is assigned as-is, with no recursive merge into the parent value (`source/utils/merge.ts:442-446`). This works at any depth. A wrapper can sit on a key the parent never set, so nothing merges it there. In that case it is unwrapped at the end by `resolveReplaceMarkers` (`source/utils/merge.ts:255-271`, `source/utils/merge.ts:489-495`).
- **`hooks`:** wrapping the whole `hooks` object merges it against `{}`, which drops every inherited hook (`source/utils/merge.ts:452-458`). You can also wrap a single hook type, such as `beforeRequest: replaceOption([...])`. That replaces only that one array (`source/utils/merge.ts:204-213`).
- **`headers`:** the new headers are merged into `{}` instead of into the inherited headers (`source/utils/merge.ts:463-467`).
- **`searchParams`:** wrapping the whole option replaces all inherited params (`source/utils/merge.ts:408-410`). Wrapping one key's value, inside an object or a `[key, value]` tuple array, deletes that key's inherited values before adding the new one (`source/utils/merge.ts:299-321`).
- **`context`:** this option is merged shallowly, so `replaceOption` is only supported around the whole `context` object. In that case the result is `{...value}` and nothing is inherited (`source/utils/merge.ts:34`, `source/utils/merge.ts:386-393`).
- **`signal`:** by default, inherited signals are combined with `AbortSignal.any`. A wrapped signal clears the inherited ones first (`source/utils/merge.ts:360-363`, `source/utils/merge.ts:476-481`). Passing `signal: undefined` instead removes them with no new signal (`source/types/options.ts:504-507`).
- **`retry`:** a wrapped `retry` skips the usual handling of a number shorthand. It is not expanded into, or merged with, the parent `retry` object (`source/utils/merge.ts:431-444`).
- **`json`:** this holds your own data, so Ky only looks for the wrapper where it replaces an inherited value (`source/utils/merge.ts:34`). If a wrapper there has nothing to replace, its `toJSON` makes it serialize as the plain value (`source/utils/merge.ts:57-58`).

One related point: to clear an inherited value without supplying a new one, you usually pass `undefined` rather than using `replaceOption`. This works for `searchParams`, `context`, single hook types and `signal` (`source/utils/merge.ts:200-201`, `source/utils/merge.ts:388-389`, `source/utils/merge.ts:405-407`).

`searchParams: undefined`, `context: undefined` clearing is cited at lines 388-389 and 405-407, which is supported, but the 'usually pass undefined' framing is the answer's own inference
questions.rationale: The answer matches the gist (marker via Symbol.for, replaces rather than merges, works for hooks, headers, searchParams, context, with the beforeRequest example) and nearly all details trace to the evidence. A few interpretive details, such as the retry behavior and the undefined-clearing advice, are inferred rather than directly stated, which is minor.

questions.question: What happens if I still pass the `prefixUrl` option?
questions.answer:
Ky refuses the request. `prefixUrl` was renamed to `prefix` in v2, and passing the old name now throws an error instead of being ignored. The tests check this with `throwsAsync`, so in practice the `ky(...)` call rejects. The error message is:

> The `prefixUrl` option has been renamed `prefix` in v2 and enhanced to allow slashes in input. See also the new `baseUrl` option for improved flexibility with standard URL resolution: https://github.com/sindresorhus/ky#baseurl

The check is near the start of the `Ky` constructor, before any options are merged or the request is built (`source/core/Ky.ts:469-471`):

```ts
if (Object.hasOwn(options, 'prefixUrl')) {
	throw new Error(prefixUrlRenamedErrorMessage);
}
```

The message is defined at `source/core/Ky.ts:63`.

**Details:**
- **The value doesn't matter.** Only the key's presence is checked, so `{prefixUrl: ''}` and even `{prefixUrl: undefined}` both throw (`test/prefix.ts:62-71`).
- **The input type doesn't matter.** It throws whether the input is a string, a `Request` or a `URL` (`test/prefix.ts:73-87`).
- **Only an "own" property counts.** Because the check uses `Object.hasOwn`, a `prefixUrl` inherited through the options object's prototype is ignored. The test builds such an object with `prefix` set and gets `/foo/bar`, using `prefix` (`test/prefix.ts:51-61`).

**How to migrate:** rename the option to `prefix`. It is joined to the input with a single `/`, with slashes trimmed where the two meet. The result is then resolved against `baseUrl` if you set one (`readme.md:251-258`). The docs recommend `baseUrl` in most cases because it follows standard URL resolution (`source/types/options.ts:151-160`).

Claim that the `prefix` is joined with a single `/` is supported by the readme, but 'docs recommend baseUrl in most cases' cites options.ts:151-160 where the text is truncated.

Nearly all claims are backed by the Ky.ts and test/prefix.ts lines shown. The only weak spots are small details, such as the claim about the check preceding option merging, and the truncated options.ts snippet cited for the baseUrl recommendation.

questions.question: How is the custom `parseJson` option used when reading a response?
questions.answer:
When `parseJson` is set, Ky reads the response body as text and passes it to your function along with `{request, response}`. When it isn't set, Ky uses `JSON.parse`. A single private helper handles this, and three places call it.

**The helper** (`source/core/Ky.ts:1007-1011`):
```ts
// Uses `parseJson` when it is set, and `JSON.parse()` otherwise.
#parseJson(text: string, request: Request, response: Response): unknown {
	const {parseJson} = this.#options;
	return parseJson ? parseJson(text, {request, response}) : JSON.parse(text);
}
```
The option docs say the same thing: your function gets the response text first and a context object with `request` and `response` second (`source/types/options.ts:55-60`).

**1. The `.json()` shortcut on the response promise** (`ky(...).json()`), in `source/core/Ky.ts:397-431`:
- Only `json` goes through this path. Other body methods call the native method directly (lines 397-399).
- Ky reads the body with `response.text()`, finds the request that actually produced this response (it can differ after a retry), and calls `#parseJson(text, request, response)` (lines 401-409).
- Empty bodies are a special case. If the body is `''`, a schema was passed and there's no custom `parseJson`, Ky skips parsing and validates `undefined` instead. With a custom `parseJson`, your function gets the empty string, which is how you handle empty bodies yourself. The `ResponsePromise` docs suggest exactly this.
- If you pass a schema, Ky validates the parsed value against it (lines 411-416). Parsing runs inside `#raceWithTotalTimeout`, so a timeout raises a `TimeoutError` (lines 406, 427-429).

**2. Replacing `Response.json()`** (`#decorateResponse`, `source/core/Ky.ts:765-780`): if `parseJson` is set, Ky overrides the response object's own `json` method:
```ts
response.json = async () => this.#parseJson(await response.text(), request, response);
```
It also wraps `clone()`, so cloned responses use your parser too instead of the native `json()` (lines 775-777). Each response is decorated only once, tracked in a set. One call site I found is the `onDownloadProgress` streaming path (`source/core/Ky.ts:657-659`). I didn't check whether it's called anywhere else.

**3. Error data on `HTTPError`** (`#getResponseData`, `source/core/Ky.ts:814-850`): for non-2xx responses, Ky reads the body text with a time limit.
- An empty body gives `undefined`.
- A body without a JSON content type is returned as plain text.
- A JSON body is parsed with `#parseJson` under a timeout. If parsing fails, the error is swallowed and the result is `undefined` (line 846).

So your `parseJson` also shapes `error.data`.

questions.question: What does the `data` property of `HTTPError` contain, and why does `error.response.json()` fail?
questions.answer:
`error.data` holds the error response body, already read and parsed for you. `error.response.json()` fails because Ky has already read that body to fill in `data`, and a fetch `Response` body can only be read once.

### How `data` is filled
When a response has a non-2xx status and `throwHttpErrors` is on, Ky creates the `HTTPError` and immediately awaits the body (`source/core/Ky.ts:632-634`):

```ts
const httpError: HTTPError = new HTTPError(currentResponse, ...);
httpError.data = await this.#getResponseData(currentResponse);
```

`#getResponseData` (`source/core/Ky.ts:814-853`) works like this:
1. It reads the body as text with `readResponseText`, with a time limit (line 830).
2. If the text is empty, `data` is `undefined` (lines 836-838).
3. If the `Content-Type` isn't JSON, `data` is the plain text string (lines 840-842).
4. If it is JSON, the text is parsed with your `parseJson` option, or `JSON.parse` by default. If parsing fails or times out, `data` is `undefined` (lines 844-852).

So its type is `T | string | undefined` (`source/errors/HTTPError.ts:20`).

The class docs (`source/errors/HTTPError.ts:9`) add some limits on reading the body:
- The read and parse are capped by the request `timeout`, or 10 s if `timeout` is disabled, by whatever is left of `totalTimeout`, and by a 10 MiB body size limit.
- If `maxResponseSize` is exceeded, Ky throws a `ResponseSizeError` instead of the `HTTPError`.
- If `totalTimeout` runs out, Ky throws a `TimeoutError` instead.
- `data` is filled before `beforeError` hooks run, so hooks can use it.

### Why `error.response.json()` fails
Filling `data` reads the body, so the body is used up by the time you catch the error. The docs say this directly (`source/errors/HTTPError.ts:11`):

> The response body is automatically consumed when populating `error.data`, so `error.response.json()` and other body methods will not work. Use `error.data` instead. The `error.response` object is still available for headers, status, etc.

### What to do instead
```ts
try {
  await ky.post(url, {json: payload});
} catch (error) {
  if (error instanceof HTTPError) {
    console.log(error.response.status); // fine: metadata is still available
    console.log(error.data);            // parsed JSON, text, or undefined
  }
}
```

questions.question: How does ky tell a dropped connection apart from other errors thrown by fetch?
questions.answer:
Ky looks at the error's type and message. When `fetch` rejects, Ky runs the error through `isRawNetworkError()` in `source/utils/is-network-error.ts`. If it matches, Ky wraps it in a `NetworkError`. Any other error is rethrown as is.

**The check** (`source/utils/is-network-error.ts:15-46`, inlined from `sindresorhus/is-network-error` v1.3.2):

1. The error must be a real `Error` whose `name === 'TypeError'` and whose `message` is a string (lines 16-23). Anything else is not a network error.
2. It then compares the message against what each runtime is known to produce:
   - **Safari 17+:** `'Load failed'` or `'Load failed (…)'`. This only counts if the error has no stack, or has a `__sentry_captured__` marker, because Sentry adds its own stack (lines 27-32).
   - **Deno:** the message starts with `'error sending request for url'` (lines 34-37).
   - **Chrome:** `'Failed to fetch'` or `'Failed to fetch (hostname)'` (lines 39-42).
   - **Other runtimes:** an exact match against a fixed list (lines 4-13, 45), which includes:
   ```ts
   'network error', // Chrome
   'NetworkError when attempting to fetch resource.', // Firefox
   'The Internet connection appears to be offline.', // Safari 16
   'fetch failed', // Undici (Node.js)
   'terminated', // Undici (Node.js)
   'Network connection lost', // Cloudflare Workers (fetch)
   ```

**Where it's used**

- **During the fetch.** In the `catch` around the fetch call, Ky first checks whether the user aborted the request and whether `totalTimeout` has run out (that case throws `TimeoutError`). Only after that does it test for a network error (`source/core/Ky.ts:1261-1272`):
  ```ts
  if (isRawNetworkError(error)) {
      throw new NetworkError(request, {cause: error as Error});
  }
  throw error;
  ```
- **While reading the body.** A connection can drop while a shortcut method like `.json()` is reading the response. That also surfaces as a raw `TypeError`, and Ky wraps it the same way, so the `beforeError` hooks run on it (`source/core/Ky.ts:902-909`).

**Why the difference matters**

- Only known error types are retried. A `NetworkError` is retried (for retriable methods), but unknown errors such as programming bugs are rethrown unless you set a `shouldRetry` override (`source/core/Ky.ts:757-762`).
- A drop during the body read is still a `NetworkError`, but Ky doesn't retry it because the response has already arrived (`source/errors/NetworkError.ts:7`).
- The original error is kept on the standard `cause` property (`source/errors/NetworkError.ts:5,15-16`).

**Limitation**

questions.question: Which HTTP methods and status codes are retried by default, and how many times?
questions.answer:
By default, Ky retries a failed request **up to 2 times**. It only retries requests using **GET, PUT, HEAD, DELETE, OPTIONS, TRACE or QUERY**, and only on status codes **408, 413, 429, 500, 502, 503 and 504**.

The defaults are set in `source/utils/normalize.ts:17-35`:

```ts
const retryMethods: HttpMethod[] = ['get', 'put', 'head', 'delete', 'options', 'trace', 'query'];
const retryStatusCodes = [408, 413, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504];
const retryAfterStatusCodes = [413, 429, 503];

const defaultRetryOptions: InternalRetryOptions = {
	limit: 2,
	methods: retryMethods,
	statusCodes: retryStatusCodes,
	afterStatusCodes: retryAfterStatusCodes,
	maxRetryAfter: Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY,
	backoffLimit: Number.POSITIVE_INFINITY,
	delay: attemptCount => 0.3 * (2 ** (attemptCount - 1)) * 1000,
	jitter: undefined,
	retryOnTimeout: false,
};
```

**Exceptions and timing:**
- **POST and PATCH are not in the default method list**, so they aren't retried unless you add them.
- **413 Payload Too Large** is only retried when the response has a retry timing header, unless `shouldRetry` returns `true` (`source/types/retry.ts:40`).
- **413, 429 and 503 follow retry timing headers.** Those are the default `afterStatusCodes`. The wait is capped by `maxRetryAfter`, which is unlimited by default (`source/types/retry.ts:46-51`).
- **Other retries use backoff.** The delay is `0.3 * 2^(attempt-1)` seconds (300ms, then 600ms, and so on). `backoffLimit` caps it and is also unlimited by default.
- **Timeouts are not retried by default** (`retryOnTimeout: false`).

**Changing the defaults:** you can pass a number as shorthand for `{limit: n}`. Any options you set are merged over the defaults, and options set to `undefined` are ignored (`source/utils/normalize.ts:37-49`). The limit must be a non-negative integer (`source/utils/normalize.ts:51-53`).
unsupported_claims: Claim that 413 is retried only when the response has a timing header is supported, but the claim that POST and PATCH are 'not retried unless you add them' is inferred rather than shown directly
Exact citation range source/types/retry.ts:46-51 for maxRetryAfter default (maxRetryAfter appears at lines 53-58)
questions.rationale: The limit, methods, status codes, afterStatusCodes, delay formula, backoffLimit, maxRetryAfter and retryOnTimeout defaults are all shown in normalize.ts and retry.ts. Minor issues are an imprecise line citation for maxRetryAfter and an inference about POST/PATCH. The answer covers all the gist's key facts except jitter, which it does not mention.

questions.question: How can I track the progress of a large file upload, and how is the total size estimated?
questions.answer:
Pass an `onUploadProgress` callback. Ky streams the request body through a progress counter and calls you with `{percent, transferredBytes, totalBytes}` plus the chunk just sent. It estimates the total from the `body` option before sending: exactly for most body types, approximately for `FormData`.

```ts
import ky from 'ky';

const response = await ky.post('https://example.com/upload', {
	body: largeFile,
	onUploadProgress: (progress, chunk) => {
		console.log(`${progress.percent * 100}% - ${progress.transferredBytes} of ${progress.totalBytes} bytes`);
	}
});
```
(`source/types/options.ts:331-345`)

**Where it doesn't run**
- It needs request-stream support from the runtime. Otherwise Ky silently ignores the callback.
- It is also ignored for requests with `keepalive: true` or `mode: 'no-cors'`.
- In Chromium-based browsers it needs an HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 connection. Streaming uploads over HTTP/1.1 fail with a network error. The fix is to retry without progress by returning `{options: {onUploadProgress: undefined}}` from a `beforeRetry` hook (`source/types/options.ts:322`, example at `source/types/hooks.ts:56-71`).
- Don't throw from the callback. A throw fails the upload with a `NetworkError`, which Ky retries, so your callback runs again. To cancel, use an `AbortController` signal (`source/types/options.ts:329`).

**How the total is estimated** (`getBodySize`, `source/utils/body.ts:29-76`)
| Body | `totalBytes` |
|---|---|
| `Blob`/`File` | `body.size` |
| `ArrayBuffer` / typed array | `byteLength` |
| string | UTF-8 encoded byte length |
| `URLSearchParams` | UTF-8 byte length of `toString()` |
| `FormData` | an approximation (see below) |
| empty or anything else | `0` (unknown) |

For `FormData`, Ky rebuilds the multipart layout itself. For each entry it counts:
- the boundary line
- the `Content-Disposition` header
- for Blob entries, the filename and `Content-Type`
- the value, with line breaks converted to CRLF
- the CRLF separators

It then adds the closing boundary (`source/utils/body.ts:34-56`). The runtime's real boundary length isn't known, so Ky uses a placeholder size (`usualFormBoundarySize`). The estimate is deliberately on the high side (except in Bun), because a low estimate would make `percent` reach its cap partway through the upload (`source/utils/body.ts:35`).

A `ReadableStream` body can't be measured. In that case Ky uses a `content-length` header if you set one. Browsers don't allow that header on requests, so in a browser the total stays `0` (`source/types/options.ts:327`).

**How the numbers are reported** (`withProgress`, `source/utils/body.ts:78-110`)
- Each chunk is reported one step late: when the next chunk arrives, the previous one is added to `transferredBytes` and reported.
- `percent` is `transferredBytes / totalBytes`, or `0` if the total is unknown. It is capped just below 1 (`1 - Number.EPSILON`), so a wrong estimate can't show 100% early.
- `totalBytes` is never reported as less than `transferredBytes`.
- When the stream finishes, a final event reports `percent: 1` with `totalBytes` set to the actual number of bytes sent. Until that event, the total is only the estimate, even if a hook replaced the request (`source/types/options.ts:327`).

I read the size estimation, the progress wrapper and the option docs, but not the code in `Ky.ts` that attaches the progress stream to the outgoing request. The support checks above come from the option's documentation, not from code I saw.

Chunks are reported one step late and the ReadableStream content-length fallback are supported, but the claim of exactness for 'most body types' is only partly shown
questions.rationale: The answer closely matches the shown getBodySize, withProgress, and option docs, and it openly says it did not read the Ky.ts wiring. The only gaps are that the stream-attachment claim comes from docs rather than code, and it omits the gist's 40-byte boundary value and the used/locked body exclusion, but it contradicts nothing.

questions.question: How are headers combined when both the instance defaults and a request set them, and how do I remove an inherited header?
questions.answer:
Headers are merged one key at a time, and the later layer wins. The instance's defaults (from `ky.create`/`.extend`) are applied first and the request's headers are laid on top. Header names are lowercased, so `Authorization` and `authorization` count as the same header. To remove an inherited header, set it to `undefined`.

**How the merge works** (`source/utils/merge.ts`)

At the top level of the options, each `headers` value is folded into the headers built up so far:

```ts
if (isRoot && isObject((source as any).headers)) {
    const {value: headerValue, isReplace} = getReplaceState((source as any).headers);
    headers = mergeHeaderContainers(isReplace ? {} : headers, headerValue as KyHeadersInit);
    returnValue.headers = headers;
}
```
(`source/utils/merge.ts:463-468`)

`mergeHeaderContainers` turns both sides into plain objects, then writes them into a `Map` keyed by the lowercased name. The second source is written last, so its values replace earlier ones (`source/utils/merge.ts:188-196`). As a result:
- Headers that only the instance sets stay as they are.
- Headers that only the request sets are added.
- When both set the same header (in any letter case), the request's value is used.
- Headers are only ever merged as a whole value per key. Values are not appended together.

You can pass headers as a `Headers` instance, a plain object or an array of pairs. Anything that isn't a plain object goes through `new Headers(...)` first, so it ends up as a plain object either way (`source/utils/merge.ts:170-184`). Hooks therefore receive a plain object with lowercase keys (`source/types/options.ts:465`).

**Removing an inherited header**

Pass the header with an `undefined` value, either to `.extend()` or to the request itself:

```ts
const original = ky.create({headers: {rainbow: 'rainbow', unicorn: 'unicorn'}});
const extended = original.extend({headers: {rainbow: undefined}});
// request.headers.has('rainbow') === false, has('unicorn') === true
```
(`source/types/options.ts:467-499`)

Things to know:
- The `undefined` value isn't deleted during the merge. It stays in the merged object as a deletion marker, so it can still remove a header that comes from a `Request` you pass as input when the request is built (`source/utils/merge.ts:186-187`; `source/types/options.ts:465`).
- A `Headers` instance can't store `undefined`. For that case only, the string `'undefined'` counts as a deletion. In a plain object, `'undefined'` is just an ordinary string value (`source/utils/merge.ts:169`, `180`; `source/types/options.ts:467`).

**Dropping all inherited headers at once**

Wrap the new headers in `replaceOption(...)`. The merge then starts from `{}` instead of the inherited headers (`isReplace ? {} : headers`, `source/utils/merge.ts:465`; `replaceOption` is defined at `source/utils/merge.ts:53-61`).

I didn't read the exact code in `source/core/Ky.ts` that turns the deletion markers into removals when the `Request` is built. That part of the answer comes from the comments and docs cited above.

The `replaceOption` behavior of starting from `{}` is supported, but the claim it applies to the request level specifically is inferred
questions.rationale: The answer matches the gist: plain-object merge, lowercase keys, later wins, undefined as a deletion marker, and the 'undefined' string for Headers instances. questions.question: How are query string parameters added to the request URL when the URL already has some?
questions.answer:
They are **merged into the URL's existing query, not used to replace it**. Ky builds the `Request` first, parses its URL, and adds the `searchParams` option to whatever query string is already there.

**Where it happens** (`source/core/Ky.ts:547-554`):

```ts
const {searchParams} = this.#options;
if (hasSearchParameters(searchParams)) {
	const url = new URL(this.request.url);
	applySearchParameters(url, searchParams);
	if (url.href !== this.request.url) {
		// rebuild the Request with the new URL
```

The `Request` is rebuilt only if the URL actually changed. Rebuilding drops a body inherited from a `Request` input, so Ky skips it when it can. When it does rebuild, it carries over request settings such as `credentials`, `mode` and `cache` from the original request (`source/core/Ky.ts:552-575`).

**How the merge works** depends on the type you pass (`applySearchParameters`, `source/core/Ky.ts:279-309`):

- **String**: a leading `?` is removed, then the string is added after the existing query with `&`. If the URL had no query, it gets `?` plus the string. An empty string does nothing (lines 290-294):
  ```ts
  url.search = url.search ? `${url.search}&${stringSearchParameters}` : `?${stringSearchParameters}`;
  ```
- **Plain object**: each entry is added with `url.searchParams.append`. A value of `undefined` removes that key from the input URL instead (lines 295-303).
- **`URLSearchParams`, arrays of key/value pairs and other accepted types**: these go through `new URLSearchParams(...)` and each pair is appended (lines 304-307).

Because the code uses `append` rather than `set`, a key that is already in the URL is **not overwritten**. You end up with both values, e.g. `?a=1&a=2`.

**Removing keys:**
- If the merged options record keys to delete (a set stored under `deletedParametersSymbol`), those keys are removed from the URL first, so later `searchParams` entries can add them back on purpose (lines 281-288). I didn't trace where that set gets filled; it's somewhere in the option merging.
- Removal checks `has()` before calling `delete()`. Calling `delete()` re-serializes the whole query, which would change an untouched URL, for example turning `%20` into `+` (lines 272-277).

**Merging across instances:** when `searchParams` comes from several option sources (e.g. `ky.extend()`), `source/utils/merge.ts:401-412` merges them before the request is built:
- `null` throws a `TypeError`.
- An explicit `undefined` clears the option.
- Later sources are merged into a `URLSearchParams`.

questions.question: Can a hook skip the network entirely and return a canned response instead?
questions.answer:
Yes. Return a `Response` from a `beforeRequest` hook and Ky won't call `fetch` at all. The hook docs say a `Response` can be returned "to completely avoid making an HTTP request". In that case the remaining `beforeRequest` hooks are skipped. The docs give mocking and checking an internal cache as example uses (`source/types/hooks.ts:149`).

```ts
const api = ky.extend({
	hooks: {
		beforeRequest: [
			() => new Response(JSON.stringify({mocked: true}), {status: 200}),
		],
	},
});
```

**How it works:**
- `#runBeforeRequestHooks` runs the hooks in order. If a hook returns a `Request`, that request replaces the outgoing one and the loop continues. If it returns a `Response`, Ky records it in `#hookResponses` and returns it straight away (`source/core/Ky.ts:1041-1062`).
- In `#run`, that response replaces the network call: `let response = beforeRequestResponse ?? await this.#retry();`. `#retry()` is the method that eventually calls fetch, and it only runs when no hook returned a response (`source/core/Ky.ts:593-598`).

**What still happens to the canned response:**
- `afterResponse` hooks still run on it (`source/core/Ky.ts:612`).
- The usual error check still applies. If the response isn't `ok`, isn't opaque, and `throwHttpErrors` is enabled, Ky builds an `HTTPError` (`source/core/Ky.ts:625-634`).
- Ky won't retry a failed response that came from a hook. Because the response is in `#hookResponses`, that `HTTPError` is thrown immediately instead of going through retry handling (`source/core/Ky.ts:607`, `638-640`).
- The response is still decorated, `onDownloadProgress` still applies to it (`source/core/Ky.ts:649-659`), and the response size limit is enforced on it (`source/core/Ky.ts:1065-1067`).

**Other hooks:**
- `afterResponse` hooks can also return a replacement `Response`, but only after a response already exists, so they can't stop the request from being sent (`source/types/hooks.ts:110`).
- A comment mentions a response "returned from a `beforeRetry` hook" (`source/core/Ky.ts:1354`), so `beforeRetry` hooks seem able to return a response in place of a retry attempt. I didn't trace that code path, so I can't confirm it.
unsupported_claims: The claim that `#retry()` is the method that eventually calls fetch is not directly shown in the visible evidence, since the body of `#retry` is truncated.

The claim that `#runBeforeRequestHooks` returns a Response straight away is supported, but the statement that the response is 'decorated' and size-limited relies on `#decorateResponse` and `#limitResponseSize` internals that are only partly visible.

questions.question: How do I use ky's XML shortcut method to parse a response into an object?
questions.answer:
ky doesn't have an XML shortcut. The response promise only offers `arrayBuffer`, `blob`, `formData`, `bytes`, `json` and `text` (`source/types/ResponsePromise.ts:9-71`). The table of media types behind those shortcuts has no XML entry either:

```ts
export const responseTypes = {
	json: 'application/json',
	text: 'text/*',
	formData: 'multipart/form-data',
	arrayBuffer: '*/*',
	blob: '*/*',
	bytes: '*/*',
} as const;
```
(`source/core/constants.ts:46-55`)

The closest option is to read the body with `.text()` and parse it yourself. In a browser you can use `DOMParser`. Outside the browser, use an XML parser library of your choice:

```ts
import ky from 'ky';

const xmlString = await ky.get(url).text();
const doc = new DOMParser().parseFromString(xmlString, 'application/xml');
```

Some details that matter here:

- **Errors:** like the other shortcuts, `.text()` throws an `HTTPError` if the status isn't in the 200–299 range (`source/types/ResponsePromise.ts:2`).
- **Accept header:** calling a shortcut directly sets an `Accept` header based on the method. For `.text()` that header is `text/*` (`source/core/constants.ts:48`). The comment above the table says these are deliberately narrow (`source/core/constants.ts:45`). A server that only serves `application/xml` may not match `text/*`. In that case, try passing `headers: {accept: 'application/xml'}` yourself. I didn't check whether an explicit `Accept` header overrides the one the shortcut sets, so test this against your server.
- **Schema validation:** only `.json()` takes a Standard Schema validator (`source/types/ResponsePromise.ts:51-67`). If you want validation with XML, run it yourself after parsing.
